function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
It will:

1. Clone the repo.  
2. Analyse the repo (we’ll assume it’s a typical Node.js app).  
3. Generate a `Dockerfile`, a Kubernetes deployment/service YAML, and a GitHub Actions workflow.  
4. Stage, commit, and push the changes.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run the commands for you, but the commands below will do everything you asked for when executed on a machine that has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl`, and `jq` installed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for nodejs-welcome
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is a lightweight base image.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` installs only production deps.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** (the common default for Node.js apps).  
> * Adjust the port if your app uses a different one.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` in the repo root:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – point to the image you’ll build/push (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, etc.).  
> * `replicas:` – adjust based on load.  
> * `type:` – switch to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            .

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * It triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds two tags: `latest` and the commit SHA.  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> * If you prefer Docker Hub or another registry, replace the login and push steps accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage, commit, and push the changes

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml

# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to remote
git push origin main
```

---

## 4️⃣ Verify

After the push completes:

1. **GitHub Actions** – Go to the *Actions* tab of the repo; you should see a successful run.  
2. **Docker image** – Check `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome` (or your chosen registry) for the `latest` tag.  
3. **Kubernetes** – If you have a cluster configured, apply the manifest:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
```

Then verify the deployment and service:

```bash
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get services
```

---

### Quick Recap

| Step | Command / File | Purpose |
|------|----------------|---------|
| 1 | `git clone ...` | Clone repo |
| 2.1 | `Dockerfile` | Build container |
| 2.2 | `k8s-deployment.yaml` | Deploy to K8s |
| 2.3 | `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` | CI/CD |
| 3 | `git add`, `git commit`, `git push` | Commit & push changes |

That’s it! 🎉 If you hit any snags (e.g., wrong image registry, port mismatch), just tweak the files accordingly. Happy coding!
